issues.legal_issue: A decree is not a nullity merely because a court exercised pecuniary jurisdiction as a result of overvaluation or undervaluation.
material_facts: The suit was valued below the amount later determined to be its correct valuation.
On the corrected valuation, the appeal from the trial court’s decree would have lain to a different court from the one that heard it.
issues.conclusion: An objection to pecuniary jurisdiction arising from overvaluation or undervaluation must be dealt with under section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act; the decree is not, for that reason alone, a nullity.
issues.legal_principle: Although a decree passed without jurisdiction is ordinarily a nullity, section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act provides a complete and exclusive procedure for objections to jurisdiction arising from overvaluation or undervaluation. Sections 21 and 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure reflect the related policy that technical jurisdictional objections should not upset a decision on the merits absent a failure of justice. Rajlakshmi Dasee v. Katyayani Dasee and Shidappa Venkatrao v. Rachappa Subrao did not determine the effect of section 11; the Privy Council’s decision in Rachappa Subrao Jadhav v. Shidappa Venkatrao Jadhav supports caution toward highly technical objections not raised at the proper time.

predicates.appeal_challenging_decree: A litigant seeks appellate review of a decree.
predicates.pecuniary_forum_error_caused_by_valuatio: A court heard a suit or appeal in a forum that would not have had pecuniary jurisdiction if the claim had been correctly valued.

issues.definition: When a litigant appeals a decree and the forum’s pecuniary jurisdiction resulted from an incorrect valuation, that valuation error alone does not make the decree a nullity.

issues.legal_issue: A change in the forum that hears an appeal, by itself, is not prejudice caused by overvaluation or undervaluation.
material_facts: Because of the valuation used, the appeal from the trial court’s decree was heard by a district court rather than the High Court.
The appellants argued that being heard by the different forum itself constituted prejudice.
issues.conclusion: A different forum for the appeal, without more, is not prejudice within the meaning of section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 requires that overvaluation or undervaluation have prejudicially affected the disposal of the case on its merits. Treating a change of appellate forum alone as prejudice would make that requirement ineffective. The Court approved the approach in Kelu Achan v. Cheriya Parvathi Nethiar, Mool Chand v. Ram Kishan, and Ramdeo Singh v. Raj Narain.

predicates.appellate_review_of_valuation_objection: An appellate court considers an objection that an incorrect valuation affected the forum’s jurisdiction.
predicates.appeal_heard_in_different_forum: An appeal was heard by a forum different from the one that would have heard it if the case had been correctly valued.

issues.definition: A change in the forum hearing an appeal, when considered in an appellate review of a valuation objection, does not by itself amount to prejudice.

issues.legal_issue: An error in a lower appellate court’s factual findings is not prejudice caused by overvaluation or undervaluation, and section 11 does not authorize a second appellate court to reconsider those findings.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the second appellate court should examine the evidence and decide the factual disputes afresh to determine prejudice.
The lower appellate court had made findings of fact after considering the evidence.
issues.conclusion: An error in factual findings cannot be treated as prejudice under section 11, and that section does not empower a second appellate court to reassess factual findings made by the lower appellate court.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act, prejudice must be directly attributable to overvaluation or undervaluation; an error in a finding reached on the evidence is not so attributable. Section 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits factual determination in the circumstances it specifies, including where the lower appellate court has failed to record a finding on an issue; it does not provide a general power to reassess findings for a section 11 inquiry. The ordinary limits on second appeals under section 100 of the Code also apply.

predicates.second_appeal: A party seeks a second appeal from a decision of a lower appellate court.
predicates.alleged_prejudice_is_error_in_lower_appe: The party alleges that the lower appellate court reached an incorrect factual finding after considering the evidence.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, an alleged error in the lower appellate court’s factual findings is not valuation-caused prejudice, and the second appellate court cannot reassess those findings for that purpose.

issues.legal_issue: Prejudice under section 11 requires a consequential failure of justice directly attributable to the valuation error, and its existence depends on the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The Court considered that valuation errors may affect the procedure available for trying a case.
The Court gave as an example a case diverted to a summary forum, where the party loses procedures and an appeal that would otherwise have been available.
The Court held that the inquiry into prejudice depends on the facts of each case.
issues.conclusion: The jurisdiction to intervene is equitable and revisional in nature and may be exercised cautiously when an erroneous assumption of jurisdiction caused by overvaluation or undervaluation results in a failure of justice; prejudice is determined on the facts of the case.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act requires prejudice to the disposal on the merits that is directly attributable to overvaluation or undervaluation. The Court described the power as an equitable, cautious, revisional jurisdiction and declined to define its limits exhaustively. A summary trial that deprives a party of significant procedural protections and an appeal may, depending on the circumstances, show such prejudice.

predicates.appellate_review_of_valuation_objection: An appellate court considers whether an incorrect valuation affected the disposal of a case.
predicates.valuation_error_caused_procedural_disadv: An incorrect valuation caused a party to lose a procedural protection or opportunity that would otherwise have been available.
predicates.disadvantage_caused_failure_of_justice: The procedural disadvantage resulting from the valuation error caused a failure of justice in the disposal of the case.

issues.definition: On appellate review of a valuation objection, a procedural disadvantage caused by the valuation error may warrant intervention when it also caused a failure of justice.

issues.legal_issue: A litigant who chose a forum on the basis of the litigant’s own valuation cannot claim prejudice merely from the resulting forum or valuation error.
material_facts: The plaintiffs instituted the suit and valued it themselves.
They pursued an appeal in the forum indicated by their valuation and did not challenge that forum’s jurisdiction until the valuation objection arose later.
The appeal in the district court received a fair and full hearing on the merits, and no resulting injustice was shown.
issues.conclusion: The appellants could not establish prejudice from the forum chosen on the basis of their own valuation; no interference was warranted, and the appeal was dismissed with costs.
issues.legal_principle: Even if the requirements relating to objections at earlier stages are construed to permit an objection in the appellate court, the requirement of prejudice remains. A party cannot claim as prejudice a consequence flowing from that party’s own act; prejudice justifying relief must result from another party’s action, not the complainant’s own choice. Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act governs the objection, consistently with the policy expressed in sections 21 and 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_decree and litigant_chose_forum_on_own_valuation and full_fair_hearing and no_injustice_shown

predicates.appeal_challenging_decree: A litigant seeks appellate review of a decree.
predicates.litigant_chose_forum_on_own_valuation: The litigant selected the valuation that determined the forum in which the litigant pursued the case or appeal.
predicates.full_fair_hearing: The challenged appeal received a fair and full hearing on the merits.
predicates.no_injustice_shown: The litigant has not shown that the challenged forum’s handling of the case caused injustice.

issues.definition: A litigant appealing a decree cannot obtain interference based on a valuation objection when the litigant chose the forum through the litigant’s own valuation, received a fair and full hearing, and shows no injustice.
